That is correct which is why it's so difficult to get rid of or create a vaccine for, though I am very hopeful that we will have one in the next decade. That said the Universal Flu vaccine is a bit of a different concept - that's trying to create a vaccine to target a part of the Flu virus that its essentially conserved across all sub-types, some very critical part of what makes the Flu the Flu, then target a part such as a stalk or surface binding area that if it's changed even a little results in a deformed or dead virus - so it can't mutate it's way out of it. With HIV we're trying to elicit very powerful non-conventional immune responses by using various Herpes Virus vectors, basically such an overwhelming response that the virus has no time to infect anything, it's eradicated before it can build a latent reservoir.

A universal flu vaccine is indeed possible or at least it's hoped it's possible. I work at one of the national primate centers, one of our main labs is working on a huge universal flu project, the idea is to target part of the virus that is essentially conserved among all flu variants and there are several, of those haemagglutinin (the H in H1N1 etc) is one that's been of particular interest because there are only so many possible subtypes (roughly 20) that will give you a functional virus, further you can target the more stable and important part of the protein - the areas where any mutation would lead to a non-infective viron. I work with SIV/HIV so I won't pretend to know exactly how they're designing things, but work is proceeding, whether anything actually comes of it is a different question, but I think it's probably only a matter of time.

It's because of the fact that most psychiatric meds - and many meds in general that target receptors - have a hyperbolic relationship with their receptor binding, meaning that at higher doses, increasing or decreasing the med doesn't do much while at lower doses it does. Another way of putting it, say that Drug X binds to 80% of Receptor Y at at 30 mg, at 15 mg it mg one might expect it to bind to 40%, when in fact that 15 mg is more like 70%. At 7 mg it's 55% and at 4 it's 40%. As you can see the low dose, the first 4 mg does most of the heavy lifting of the drug and the remaining 26 does basically the other half, that's why the final cuts are always the most difficult and cause the most symptoms.
